results.claim: The tuples a=(2,3,5,12) and b=(1,1,1,4,6,9) satisfy the positive-integer hypotheses, and their Landau function is 1-periodic.
results.proof_sketch: Both tuples are nonempty and contain only positive integers. Their sums are both 22. For every real x, floor(n(x+1))=floor(nx)+n, so L(x+1)=L(x)+sum(a)-sum(b)=L(x). Consequently, checking L on [0,1) suffices for every real x≥0.

results.claim: These tuples satisfy L(x)≥0 for every real x≥0.
results.proof_sketch: The denominator breakpoints in (0,1), paired with their exact L-values, are (1/9,0), (1/6,0), (2/9,0), (1/4,0), (1/3,0), (4/9,1), (1/2,1), (5/9,0), (2/3,2), (3/4,2), (7/9,1), (5/6,2), (8/9,1). Also L(0)=0. Between consecutive denominator breakpoints, the denominator floors are constant and the numerator floors are nondecreasing. Thus the minimum on each such half-open interval occurs at its left endpoint. Every listed value is nonnegative, proving the condition throughout [0,1), including its discontinuities. Periodicity proves it for all real x≥0.

results.claim: The corresponding q-factorial ratio is D(q)=[10]_q[11]_q(1-q²+q⁴), a polynomial in Z[q] of degree 23.
results.proof_sketch: Using [1]_q!=1 and cancelling factorials gives D(q)=[2]_q[10]_q[11]_q[12]_q/([4]_q[6]_q). Since [12]_q/[6]_q=1+q⁶ and [4]_q/[2]_q=1+q², the remaining quotient is (1+q⁶)/(1+q²)=1-q²+q⁴. This proves the stated polynomial identity and degree 9+10+4=23.

results.claim: The complete coefficient sequence of (1+q)D(q), indexed from 0 through 24, is (1,3,4,4,5,7,9,11,13,15,16,15,14,15,16,15,13,11,9,7,5,4,4,3,1).
results.proof_sketch: Let t_k denote the coefficient of q^k in [10]_q[11]_q. For 0≤k≤19, t_k=min(k+1,10,20-k), and t_k=0 outside this range. Expanding (1+q)(1-q²+q⁴)[10]_q[11]_q gives c_k=t_k+t_{k-1}-t_{k-2}-t_{k-3}+t_{k-4}+t_{k-5}, yielding the displayed sequence. An independent exact calculation also verified that the original denominator q-factorial product multiplied by D equals the original numerator q-factorial product.

results.claim: The displayed coefficient sequence is not unimodal, providing a complete refutation of the recorded conjecture.
results.proof_sketch: Its coefficients satisfy c_10=16, c_12=14, and c_14=16. If a unimodal peak index h were at least 12, the nondecreasing prefix would require c_10≤c_12, which is false. If h<12, the nonincreasing suffix would require c_12≥c_14, which is also false. Thus no peak index exists. The tuples satisfy every hypothesis, so this is a counterexample to the original recorded conclusion.

final_writeup:
The conjecture is false. Take a=(2,3,5,12) and b=(1,1,1,4,6,9).

All entries are positive integers, and both tuples sum to 22. Therefore their Landau function

L(x)=floor(2x)+floor(3x)+floor(5x)+floor(12x)-3floor(x)-floor(4x)-floor(6x)-floor(9x)

is 1-periodic. Its denominator breakpoints in (0,1), with exact values of L, are:

(1/9,0), (1/6,0), (2/9,0), (1/4,0), (1/3,0), (4/9,1), (1/2,1), (5/9,0), (2/3,2), (3/4,2), (7/9,1), (5/6,2), (8/9,1).

Also L(0)=0. Between these breakpoints, denominator floors remain constant while numerator floors can only increase. Hence L≥0 throughout [0,1), including every breakpoint. Periodicity establishes the required hypothesis for EVERY real x≥0.

Cancelling the q-factorials gives

D(q)=[2]_q[10]_q[11]_q[12]_q/([4]_q[6]_q)
     =[10]_q[11]_q(1-q²+q⁴).

Thus D belongs to Z[q] and has degree 23. The complete coefficient sequence of (1+q)D is

(1,3,4,4,5,7,9,11,13,15,16,15,14,15,16,15,13,11,9,7,5,4,4,3,1).

In particular, c_10=16>c_12=14<c_14=16. A unimodal sequence cannot have this strict valley: a peak at or after 12 contradicts the first inequality, and a peak before 12 contradicts the second. This proves a full refutation.
